meta.name: Borzoi First Year Costs
meta.excerpt: Borzoi first-year costs run $4,000–$9,550 including purchase price. Fencing investment can be significant for this sighthound. Gastropexy at spay/neuter is strongly recommended given the bloat risk.
meta.meta_description: Borzoi first year costs: puppy price $1,500–$3,000, secure fencing investment, vet bills including gastropexy recommendation, insurance for sighthound...

intro.label: Acquisition & Setup Costs
intro.heading: What You'll Pay to Bring a Borzoi Home
intro.html:
A Borzoi puppy from a health-tested breeder typically runs $1,500–$3,000, which puts the breed in a more accessible price band than many rare or trendy sighthounds. The Borzoi Club of America keeps a breeder referral list, and it's worth using it — a serious breeder will hand you OFA hip results, a current CAER eye clearance, and a cardiac evaluation before you ever discuss a deposit. Expect a real conversation, not just a sale. Because Borzoi cannot safely live off-leash outside a fenced enclosure, responsible breeders routinely ask about your property, your fence, and whether you've owned a sighthound before. That screening protects the dog, but it also means you should have your infrastructure sorted before you start calling breeders, not after.

Rescue adoption runs $150–$400 through Borzoi-specific or general sighthound rescue groups. Many of the adult dogs available through rescue didn't fail because they were difficult — they landed in rescue because an owner underestimated what 'never off-leash' actually means day to day, or didn't anticipate the breed's aloof, low-interaction temperament and wanted something more demonstrative. If you're comfortable with a quiet, independent, cat-like housemate and you already have secure fencing, rescue is a genuinely good route for this breed, and it sidesteps a meaningful chunk of the acquisition cost.

Setting Up the House

Initial setup costs run $300–$550, not counting fencing, and the line items skew larger than a typical medium-breed shopping list because Borzoi are long dogs, not just tall ones:

  • Large/XL crate (42–48 inches, needed even before the dog reaches full adult length): $80–$150
  • XL dog bed — a standard 'large breed' bed is often too short for an adult Borzoi to stretch out in: $70–$130
  • Collar, harness, and a proper long leash for controlled decompression walks: $60–$100
  • Grooming tools — pin brush, wide-tooth comb, detangling spray for the feathered coat: $50–$100
  • Bowls: $30–$60

Fencing Is Not Optional

If your property doesn't already have suitable fencing, budget $500–$3,000+ for this before you bring a Borzoi home. It is the single largest infrastructure line item most owners face, and it's non-negotiable rather than a nice-to-have. A Borzoi's prey drive fires instantly and their top speed clears 40 mph — a gap in a fence, or a fence low enough to see over, is enough for a dog to be gone before you finish calling its name. The standard is a solid 6-foot fence with no sightlines to squirrels, rabbits, or neighborhood cats on the other side; chain-link that a dog can see through tends to encourage fence-running and frustration even when it physically contains the dog. Suburban and rural buyers installing new fencing from scratch land toward the top of that range; owners in dense urban areas sometimes solve this with a securely fenced dog run or a converted portion of a small yard rather than fencing an entire lot, which can bring the cost down but rarely eliminates it.

Regional price variation matters here more than it does for most breeds. A breeder in the Midwest or South may price Borzoi litters $300–$500 lower than a comparable breeder in a major coastal metro, while fencing contractors in expensive urban markets can run 30–50% higher per linear foot than in rural areas. It's worth getting a fencing quote before you commit to a breeder or a rescue, since it can shift your realistic total acquisition budget by thousands of dollars either direction.

care.label: First-Year Recurring Expenses
care.heading: Feeding, Vet Care, and Grooming Through Year One
care.html:
The first twelve months of Borzoi ownership don't spend evenly — costs cluster early, then taper. Thinking of it as a timeline makes the budgeting easier than treating it as one lump sum.

Month by Month

Months 1–3 are the heaviest: the crate, XL bed, leash, bowls, and grooming kit all get bought at once, fencing goes in if it isn't already there, and you're covering the first wellness exam plus the early puppy vaccination series. This stretch is where most of that $300–$550 setup budget and any fencing spend actually lands.

Months 4–6 bring the spay or neuter appointment ($200–$500), and this is the visit where you should be discussing prophylactic gastropexy with your vet — an additional $200–$500 tacked onto the same anesthesia event. Borzoi are deep-chested and genuinely at risk for bloat (GDV), and having the stomach tacked while the dog is already under for the spay/neuter is far cheaper and far safer than treating an emergency rotation later. This is also the window for finishing core vaccines, starting basic obedience work, and beginning heartworm/flea prevention if it wasn't started earlier.

Months 7–12 settle into a steadier rhythm: monthly parasite prevention, insurance premiums, food, and possibly your first lure coursing or fast-CAT entry fees as the dog matures enough for organized speed events. Nothing dramatic should be happening financially in this stretch if the earlier months were handled — which is exactly the point of front-loading the setup and gastropexy decisions.

Food Math for a 60–105 lb Dog

Food costs $600–$900 for the first year, or roughly $50–$80 a month. At adult size, a Borzoi eats somewhere around 4–6 cups of a large-breed formula daily depending on weight, metabolism, and activity — a 60-lb bitch eats notably less than a 105-lb dog. Split that into two meals rather than one; twice-daily feeding is a genuine bloat-risk-reduction measure for a deep-chested breed, not just a feeding preference. Puppies eat a large-breed puppy formula that supports controlled, steady growth rather than rapid bulking — sighthounds do better maturing slowly, and most owners transition to adult food somewhere between 12 and 18 months rather than the 9-12 months typical of smaller breeds. Store kibble in an airtight bin away from heat and light; a large dog goes through a bag fast enough that freshness is rarely an issue, but it's still worth checking the bag date at purchase.

Veterinary Care

First-year veterinary costs run $500–$900, covering the wellness exam and vaccine series ($150–$350), spay/neuter with or without gastropexy ($200–$500, plus the gastropexy add-on if elected), and heartworm/parasite prevention sized for a large dog ($150–$250/year). One detail specific to this breed: every vet who touches your Borzoi — for a dental cleaning, a torn nail, an unrelated surgery, anything requiring sedation — needs to know it's a sighthound before they draw up anesthesia. Borzoi metabolize certain anesthetic drugs differently than most breeds because of low body fat and unique liver enzyme activity, and a standard dosing protocol can be dangerous. Bring this up, in writing if you have to, at every clinic that isn't your regular vet.

Insurance

Pet insurance runs $600–$1,200/year, and for a Borzoi it's less optional than it is for many breeds, given the combined anesthesia sensitivity and bloat risk. Enroll before the first vet visit rather than after a diagnosis, and read the GDV/bloat exclusion language carefully — this is the condition most likely to generate a genuine four-figure emergency bill for this breed, and you want to know before you need it that the policy actually pays out for it.

Grooming the Silky Coat

Grooming runs $0–$400/year, and this is one place where Borzoi are cheaper than their glamorous appearance suggests. The long, silky coat needs brushing 2–3 times a week to manage shedding and keep the feathering on the legs, tail, and chest from tangling, but it doesn't mat the way a Poodle or Bearded Collie coat does, and it never needs clipping, hand-stripping, or a specialized cut. A one-time $50–$100 investment in a pin brush, wide-tooth comb, and detangling spray covers a fully adequate home routine for the dog's entire life. Some owners add professional bathing every 6–8 weeks at $60–$120 a session purely for convenience — worth it if you're short on time or don't have a tub big enough for a 90-lb dog, but not required.

If you get into lure coursing or fast-CAT, budget an extra $50–$200/year in entry fees. It's money well spent: these events give the breed the short, explosive sprint work its body is built for, in a fenced, controlled setting — exactly the exercise pattern a Borzoi actually needs, rather than the sustained jogging or fetch routines that suit other breeds.

special.label: Total Cost & Long-Term Outlook
special.heading: Total First-Year Investment and What Comes After
special.html:
First-year total: $4,000–$9,550, purchase price included. The spread is wide mainly because of fencing — an owner who already has a secure 6-foot fence and buys a lower-priced puppy lands near the bottom; an owner installing fencing from scratch, paying breeder prices at the top of the range, and adding full insurance plus gastropexy lands near the top.

Two Realistic Paths

A budget-conscious first year might look like: rescue adoption ($150–$400) + existing or minimal fencing repairs (~$500) + basic setup ($300) + food ($600) + core vet care without gastropexy ($500) + no insurance or a bare-bones policy (~$400) — landing around $2,250–$2,700. It's workable, but skipping insurance and gastropexy on a breed with real bloat and anesthesia risk is a trade-off, not a savings.

A fuller first year looks like: breeder puppy at the top of the range ($3,000) + full fencing install ($2,500) + complete setup ($550) + food ($900) + vet care with gastropexy ($900) + robust insurance ($1,200) + lure coursing entries ($200) — around $9,250, close to the top of the stated range. Most owners land somewhere in between, closer to $5,000–$6,500.

One-Time vs. Recurring Costs at a Glance

CostTypeRange
Puppy/adoptionOne-time$150–$3,000
FencingOne-time$500–$3,000+
Crate, bed, leash, bowls, grooming kitOne-time$300–$550
Spay/neuter + gastropexyOne-time$200–$1,000
FoodRecurring (annual)$600–$900
Preventives & routine vetRecurring (annual)$350–$600
InsuranceRecurring (annual)$600–$1,200
GroomingRecurring (annual)$0–$400

Where the Real Risk Lives

Three health scenarios drive most of the financial uncertainty in Borzoi ownership, and they're worth budgeting around specifically rather than in the abstract. GDV (bloat), if gastropexy wasn't done, is an emergency-room event requiring surgery within hours — $3,000–$8,000, and a dog without insurance or savings set aside for it is genuinely at risk of not getting timely treatment. Osteosarcoma, a bone cancer with elevated incidence in large/giant sighthounds, can run $5,000–$15,000+ depending on whether the owner pursues amputation, chemotherapy, or a more conservative palliative approach. Cardiac conditions caught on the puppy-stage evaluation or later in life carry variable, sometimes ongoing, management costs. None of these are likely in any given year, but across a 9–14 year lifespan the odds that at least one comes up are not negligible, which is the actual argument for insurance rather than a hypothetical one.

Money-Saving Tactics That Don't Cut Corners

  • Do the gastropexy at the same anesthesia event as the spay/neuter — it's the cheapest point in the dog's life to eliminate a $3,000–$8,000 future emergency.
  • Skip professional grooming entirely; the coat genuinely doesn't need it, and the DIY tool investment pays for itself within the first year.
  • Get a fencing quote before committing to a puppy price at the top of the breeder range — sometimes the better financial move is a slightly less expensive litter and a better fence, not the reverse.
  • Look at rescue if you already have secure fencing and sighthound experience — it removes the $1,500–$3,000 acquisition cost entirely without asking you to compromise on the dog's needs.

Two false economies specific to this breed: skipping pet insurance because the dog seems healthy as a puppy (bloat and osteosarcoma risk don't show up until later, when premiums for a diagnosed condition are no longer available), and using a low or unrated fence contractor to save money on a job where the entire point is that it cannot fail even once.

Long-Term Ongoing Costs

Annual costs after year one settle to roughly $1,550–$2,700: food ($600–$900), routine vet care and preventives ($350–$600), insurance ($600–$1,200), and grooming (minimal at home, or $400–$800 if you keep up professional bathing). Across a 9–14 year lifespan, total ownership cost excluding the original purchase price and fencing typically lands between $15,000–$35,000, with the spread driven almost entirely by whether — and how — the major health risks above end up playing out.

faq.q: Is fencing genuinely non-negotiable for a Borzoi owner?
faq.a: Yes. It's usually the single largest first-year expense outside the puppy price itself, and there's no substitute for it — Borzoi cannot be reliably recalled off-leash once prey drive triggers, and their top speed near 40 mph means a gap or a low fence is enough to lose the dog permanently. A solid 6-foot fence with no sightlines to squirrels or cats is the standard. Price this out before you commit to a breeder or rescue; it can shift your total budget by thousands depending on whether your property already has it.

faq.q: Why does pet insurance matter more for this breed than for many others?
faq.a: Borzoi carry two overlapping risks that make insurance less optional: anesthesia sensitivity, which means any sedation event — planned or emergency — needs sighthound-specific dosing, and elevated bloat (GDV) risk from their deep chest. GDV surgery alone runs $3,000–$8,000 and must happen within hours of symptoms appearing. Enroll before the first vet visit, not after a scare, and confirm the policy actually covers GDV and cardiac conditions rather than assuming it does.

faq.q: Does the long coat make grooming expensive?
faq.a: Less than it looks. The silky coat doesn't mat the way some long-coated breeds' do, and it never needs clipping or hand-stripping. A pin brush, wide-tooth comb, and detangling spray — around $50–$100 total — cover a full home routine for the dog's life, with brushing 2–3 times a week. Professional bathing every 6–8 weeks ($60–$120 a visit) is a convenience some owners add, not a requirement. The real cost here is time, not money.

faq.q: Should I do gastropexy even if it costs extra at the spay/neuter appointment?
faq.a: Most vets familiar with deep-chested breeds recommend it strongly. The $200–$500 add-on, done under the same anesthesia as the spay or neuter, tacks the stomach in place and essentially removes the risk of fatal GDV rotation later in life — a condition that otherwise costs $3,000–$8,000 to treat as an emergency and carries real mortality risk if surgery isn't fast enough. It's one of the few single decisions in a Borzoi's first year with an outsized effect on lifetime risk.

faq.q: How much of the first-year total actually depends on where I live?
faq.a: More than you'd expect for a dog breed article. Fencing contractors in dense urban or coastal markets can run 30–50% higher per foot than in rural or Midwestern areas, and breeder prices for the same quality of health testing vary $300–$500 or more by region. If you're comparing your own budget to the ranges given here, get a local fencing quote and check regional breeder pricing before assuming you'll land in the middle of the stated range.
